interest: Indexes 1930s US Canal Zone coordination, including the Interdepartmental Intelligence Liaison Board and British protest over the 1934 fleet transit.
overview: Decimal file 894.20219 contains the State Department's official List of Papers (Form DS-46) documenting diplomatic, military, and naval correspondence between 1933 and 1939 regarding Japanese military activities, intelligence gathering, espionage, and propaganda in the Republic of Panama and the Canal Zone. The records track growing American security concerns over alleged Japanese espionage adjacent to the Panama Canal, covert surveillance by Japanese naval vessels and undercover agents, and fears of sabotage during the transit of the United States Fleet in April 1934. The file details extensive inter-agency cooperation among the State, War, and Navy Departments, including the creation of the Coordinated Protective Information Service and the Interdepartmental Intelligence Liaison Board in Panama. Additionally, the papers document diplomatic tensions arising from the temporary closure of the Canal to commercial traffic during fleet transit, resulting in formal protests from the British government regarding treaty rights under the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, as well as broader surveillance of Japanese commercial concessions, travel, and suspected covert operations throughout Central America and northern South America.

subfiles.about: Official Department of State docket register (Form DS-46) listing and summarizing correspondence, despatches, telegrams, and memoranda filed under decimal file 894.20219 concerning Japanese military and espionage activities in Panama and neighboring regions from 1933 to 1939.
subfiles.summary: This 15-page document comprises the Department of State's official List of Papers (Form DS-46) docketing correspondence and reports under decimal file 894.20219 between 1933 and 1939. It outlines intelligence reports and diplomatic correspondence concerning Japanese espionage and activities in Panama, defense measures and precautions against sabotage taken by the Governor of the Panama Canal, and security protocols surrounding the continuous transit of the U.S. Fleet in April 1934. It further chronicles the ensuing diplomatic dispute with Great Britain over commercial shipping delays and treaty rights under the Hay-Pauncefote Treaty, inter-agency coordination between State, War, and Navy creating the Interdepartmental Intelligence Liaison Board, and investigations into Japanese commercial and intelligence operations throughout Central America and northern South America.
